clue.text: Medium-weight seventeenth-century dramatist

parts.note: medium means middle, as in a middle size
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A boxer's weight class seems to describe a Jacobean playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medium-weight' reads like a boxing division, but it splits into two pieces. Thomas Middleton wrote The Changeling and Women Beware Women.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Middleton was a Jacobean playwright, author of The Revenger's Tragedy and The Changeling.

clue.text: He had the gall to cure his own blindness

definitions.text: He had the gall to cure his own blindness

parts.words: He had the gall to cure his own blindness
parts.note: in the apocryphal Book of ... a blind father's sight is restored with the gall of a fish; 'had the gall' also suggests cheek

explanation.surface: Someone has the nerve to treat their own failing sight.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Apocrypha the blind patriarch is healed when fish gall is rubbed on his eyes.

clue.text: Quotes for unreliable pie charts

indicators.note: something unreliable cannot be trusted to stay as it is, so the letters of pie are rearranged

parts.note: charts are graphs

explanation.surface: A complaint that pie charts can mislead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unreliable' scrambles the first word only; 'pie charts' looks like one phrase but splits in two, the second word giving a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Epigraphs are short quotations placed at the head of a book or chapter.

clue.text: Victorian poet portrays animals round stream

indicators.note: the animals are placed round the stream, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: swine are pigs, animals
a burn is a Scottish word for a stream

explanation.surface: A Victorian poet writes about beasts by a brook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' wraps the animals about the stream. A burn is the Scottish word for a brook; Swinburne wrote Poems and Ballads.
explanation.definitionFit: Algernon Charles Swinburne was a leading poet of the later nineteenth century.

clue.text: One of Kipling's brought the bread you eat

definitions.text: One of Kipling's brought the bread you eat

parts.words: One of Kipling's brought the bread you eat
parts.note: Kipling's poem Big ... has the ships say they are going to fetch you your bread and your butter

explanation.surface: Something of Kipling's delivered the bread on your table.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's poem shows the big merchant ships carrying food to Britain.

clue.text: A.S. Byatt's eponymous creatures in dissenting bodies

parts.note: sects are groups that have broken away from a church

explanation.surface: Byatt's title creatures are found among nonconformist congregations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link word but gives its own letters. Byatt's book is Angels and Insects.
explanation.definitionFit: Byatt's novella collection Angels and Insects names the creatures in its title.

clue.text: The beautiful Italian Miss Wilfer ()

explanation.surface: An Italian beauty is a Dickens heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Bella means beautiful in Italian, and Bella Wilfer is the heroine of Dickens's Our Mutual Friend.

clue.text: Land of Hope, and slightly tarnished Glory

definitions.text: Land of Hope, and slightly tarnished Glory

parts.words: Land of Hope, and slightly tarnished Glory
parts.note: the patriotic song title is split: Anthony Hope invented this faded kingdom in The Prisoner of Zenda

explanation.surface: A patriotic song title, slightly spoiled.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Hope set The Prisoner of Zenda in an imaginary central European kingdom of faded splendour.

clue.text: Try a cut of lamb, say

explanation.surface: Sample a slice of lamb, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb is Charles Lamb, author of the Essays of Elia, so a piece of his writing is one of his works.
explanation.definitionFit: To try is to attempt; a short prose piece such as Charles Lamb wrote is the same word.

clue.text: Capital Irish folk portrayed by Joyce

definitions.text: Capital Irish folk portrayed by Joyce

parts.words: Capital Irish folk portrayed by Joyce
parts.note: the people of Ireland's capital city are the subject of Joyce's 1914 story collection

explanation.surface: Excellent Irish people in Joyce's portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce's story collection depicts citizens of Ireland's capital.

clue.text: Sporting arena associated with Masters by A. G. Macdonell?

explanation.surface: A sports ground linked with the masters in Macdonell's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground, scene of a famous match in Macdonell's England, Their England.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord's is the cricket ground in London; lords are masters or rulers.

clue.text: Part of Grace Paley's same day

definitions.text: Part of Grace Paley's same day

parts.words: Part of Grace Paley's same day
parts.note: Paley's story collection is titled with this word followed by the same day

explanation.surface: A portion of one day in a Grace Paley book.
explanation.definitionFit: Grace Paley's 1985 collection is Later the Same Day, meaning afterwards on that day.

clue.text: Cry "ham act!" possibly, as theatre critic

indicators.note: possibly says the letters could be arranged otherwise, so they are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A critic heckles a hammy performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges CRY plus HAMACT. Desmond MacCarthy was a leading drama critic.
explanation.definitionFit: Desmond MacCarthy reviewed plays for the New Statesman.

clue.text: Big lie identifies friend of Felix Salten's forest dweller

definitions.text: friend of Felix Salten's forest dweller

explanation.surface: A whopper exposes a companion of Bambi.
explanation.definitionFit: A whopping falsehood is a thumping one, and the rabbit befriends the young deer of Salten's Bambi.

clue.text: Lucian (the revised edition) is improper

indicators.note: a revised edition reworks the text, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A new edition of Lucian is judged indecent.
explanation.definitionFit: Unethical conduct is morally wrong, which is what improper means here.

clue.text: Misdemeanour includes Latin from Points for Italian People

indicators.note: one word includes another, so it goes round it

parts.note: a sin is a wrongdoing
ab is the Latin word for from
E and S are compass points, east and south

explanation.surface: An offence involves Latin taken from a book about Italians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' puts the Latin for 'from' inside the wrongdoing, then two compass points follow. 'Points for Italian People' sounds like a book title, but it is wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sabines lived in central Italy and were absorbed by early Rome.

clue.text: Desert resort for tourists, last resort for Elijah

explanation.surface: A desert town is a holiday spot and also the prophet's refuge.
explanation.definitionFit: Beersheba is a Negev city visited by travellers, and Elijah fled there from Jezebel in 1 Kings 19.

clue.text: She's set on nonsense from Maupassant's freethinking uncle

indicators.note: nonsense means the words are garbled, so they are reshuffled

parts.note: she's, read as she is, keeps its final s as a letter

explanation.surface: A woman is fixed on gibberish from a French story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nonsense' rearranges SHES, SET and ON. Maupassant's tale is Mon oncle Sosthène.
explanation.definitionFit: Maupassant's story Mon oncle Sosthene concerns an anticlerical, freethinking uncle.

clue.text: Admiral holds one Scandinavian writer

clue.text: Musical girl twice warned

parts.note: the 1925 musical comedy title gives the heroine's name after a doubled no

explanation.surface: A girl in a show gets a double warning.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical No, No, Nanette puts a double refusal before its heroine's name.

clue.text: Frenzied women reform — amend as bacchantes

indicators.note: to reform is to make over, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Wild women are urged to change their ways as followers of Bacchus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' rearranges AMEND AS; bacchantes repeats the sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Maenads were the ecstatic female followers of Dionysus.

clue.text: Spoil written work of Shakespearean vicar

parts.note: to mar is to spoil
a text is a written work

explanation.surface: Damage a written piece by a vicar.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Oliver Martext is the country priest in As You Like It.

clue.text: Feminist writer reportedly member of US fraternity

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, so the word is said aloud

parts.note: a Shriner belongs to the Shriners, an American Masonic fraternity

explanation.surface: A feminist author is said to belong to an American lodge.
explanation.walkthrough: Olive Schreiner wrote The Story of an African Farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive Schreiner was a South African novelist and campaigner for women's rights.

clue.text: Measures taken by Kosinski ()

explanation.surface: Measures taken by an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Steps are measures or actions, and Steps is a 1968 novel by Jerzy Kosinski.

clue.text: Nurse never without her gamp

parts.note: Dickens's drunken nurse Mrs Gamp, of Martin Chuzzlewit, always carries an umbrella, which came to be called a gamp

explanation.surface: A nurse always carries her umbrella.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Gamp's first name in Martin Chuzzlewit, and gamp became slang for an umbrella.

clue.text: Sort of route booked by Malraux

definitions.text: Sort of route booked by Malraux

parts.words: Sort of route booked by Malraux
parts.note: Malraux's novel La Voie ... names a kind of road

explanation.surface: A type of road put in a French novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Malraux's 1930 novel is La Voie royale, The Royal Way.

clue.text: Peacock character from old crone's cottage

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A character emerges from an old woman's cottage.
explanation.walkthrough: Peacock is Thomas Love Peacock; Mr Escot is in his novel Headlong Hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Escot is the pessimist philosopher in Thomas Love Peacock's Headlong Hall.

clue.text: His achievements are history

parts.note: reads as a man whose successes are past, but the historian's achievements were works of history

explanation.surface: A man whose glory days are over.
explanation.definitionFit: G. M. Trevelyan wrote English Social History and other major historical works.

clue.text: "Her complexion really was as pure as — Parian marble" (Thackeray, The Virginians)

definitions.text: "Her complexion really was as pure as — Parian marble" (Thackeray, The Virginians)

parts.words: "Her complexion really was as pure as — Parian marble" (Thackeray, The Virginians)
parts.note: the missing word in Thackeray's sentence is an adjective meaning shining

explanation.surface: A line from Thackeray with one word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The rare adjective means brilliant or gleaming, fitting polished marble.

clue.text: Fleet assembly point in Gaul is described by Racine

indicators.note: in says the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A naval mustering place in Gaul appears in Racine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek fleet gathered at Aulis before Troy; Racine's Iphigenie is set there.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek fleet mustered at this Boeotian port before sailing for Troy.
